title: Lacson asks: Why settle unpaid 2024 DSWD guarantee letters in 2027?
summary: Service providers reportedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents belatedly, which is why the special provision was only proposed in the 2027 budget bill

blocks.text: Service providers reportedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents belatedly, which is why the special provision was only proposed in the 2027 budget bill

items: Senator Panfilo Lacson raised concerns about a special provision in the House version of the 2027 budget bill that allocates funds to pay off unpaid guarantee letters issued by the DSWD in 2024 for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program.
Senator Risa Hontiveros explained that the DSWD was surprised by the late filing of claims by service providers, which led to the need for this special provision.
The DSWD plans to temporarily suspend the issuance of guarantee letters for AICS starting November 30.

MANILA, Philippines – Senator Panfilo Lacson flagged the proposed special provision in the House of Representatives’ version of the 2027 budget bill to pay off unpaid guarantee letters (GLs) issued by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) three years ago.
Lacson raised the issue during plenary deliberations on the DSWD’s proposed 2027 budget on Wednesday, November 25.
He pointed out that the House version of the DSWD budget includes a special provision for the “protective services program for individuals and families in difficult circumstances.”

It states that the amount for the program “shall likewise be used for the payment of arrears to accredited and/or partner service providers arising from the issuance of Guarantee Letter (GL) in FY (fiscal year) 2024, subject to the availability of funds and compliance with applicable budgeting, accounting, and auditing laws, rules and regulations.”

The GLs are for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) program, which provides financial assistance for medical needs, burial, transportation, education, food, and other support services or needs of a person or family.
Lacson noted that the allotment of over P34 billion for AICS in 2024 was fully obligated.

“So you’re issuing guarantee letters over and beyond what is authorized under GAA (General Appropriations Act) or under the law to spend under AICS. Mahirap maintindihan (This is difficult to understand), Mr. [Senate] President,” Lacson said.

Senator Risa Hontiveros, the DSWD’s budget sponsor, said service providers belatedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents, which is why the special provision was only proposed in the 2027 budget bill.

“Nagulat din ang department. By the time dumating ‘yong mga GL, wala na pong pondo. Kasi hindi nila ino-obligate pagka-issue ng GL, pagka lamang ginamit na talaga at may billing na mula sa mga ospital,” Hontiveros said.

(The department was also surprised. By the time the GLs arrived, there were no available funds left. The department doesn’t obligate the funds when GLs are issued; only after the GLs are used and hospitals have sent the billing.)
The value of unpaid claims from the guarantee letters was not mentioned.
Asked whether the GLs were issued by lawmakers, Hontiveros clarified that it was the DSWD itself that issued the letters.

“Nagsi-signify ang department na handa sila kung sakaling hindi natin tanggapin na magkaroon ng special provision. Itutuloy ‘yong money claims process. Nga lamang, siyempre matagal ‘yon, at magkakaroon kaagad ng epekto na hindi tatanggapin,” she said.

(The department is signifying that it’s ready just in case the Senate won’t accept the inclusion of a special provision. It’ll just continue with the money claims process. It’s just that the process would be long and the possible effect would be the service providers may not agree with it.)
Learning from the ordeal, Hontiveros said, the DSWD will ensure early liquidation of guarantee letters moving forward, so there would be enough time to settle payments to service providers.

On Monday, November 23, the DSWD said it will temporarily suspend the issuance of guarantee letters for AICS starting November 30. The expected resumption will be on the first working day in January 2027.
This will not affect the availment of outright payment of cash aid to AICS beneficiaries.

“The DSWD will continue to accommodate individuals and families experiencing crisis situations who need immediate financial assistance through its field offices and satellite offices nationwide,” it said in a statement.
Civil society groups criticize the AICS program as “soft pork” being weaponized for political patronage.
During his interpellation, Lacson said he wants to break down the funding for AICS into the DSWD’s sub-programs. He described AICS as “whimsical.”

“Kung sino ‘yong marunong lumapit sa mga politiko, ‘yon ang mga mauuna. Kaya nga minsan naka-hikaw ng ginto eh, hindi talaga nangangailangan, wala talaga sa crisis situations, nakakakuha sila ng biyaya galing sa AICS,” he claimed.

(Only the people who know how to approach politicians are being prioritized. That’s why sometimes those who receive aid from the AICS program are not really needy, not really in crisis situations, or they even wear gold earrings.)
Hontiveros assured Lacson that the DSWD has full control over the decision-making and disbursement of aid under the program.
Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), AICS was allocated P33.29 billion. The House added P25 billion.
While the DSWD earlier appealed to senators for a P63-billion budget for AICS, the Senate finance committee only recommended P48 billion.

During a committee hearing in October, Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said restoring the budget to P63 billion, the same level in the 2026 budget, will help them support Filipinos affected by El Niño, inflation, and other crises in 2027.
The Senate panel realigned the AICS budget to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation or PhilHealth.
As a whole, the DSWD and its attached agencies have P253.34 billion for proposed general appropriations under the Senate committee report.
That figure is P12 billion higher than the P241.28 billion in the NEP, but P9.42 billion lower than the P262.76 billion in the House budget measure. – Rappler.com
